lesson.title: One Input, One Answer: The Rule That Defines a Function
lesson.summary: A function is a special kind of relation where every input produces exactly one output, a single rule that makes functions predictable and reliable to work with.
lesson.body:
A function is a relation with one extra rule attached: every input is allowed to produce exactly one output, no more and no less. Recall that a relation is any set of ordered pairs connecting inputs to outputs, without restriction; some relations let a single input branch off into multiple different outputs. A function refuses to allow that. If you feed the same input into a function twice, you must get the identical output both times, every single time. This single requirement is what makes functions so useful and predictable, because once you know a function's rule and an input, you can always be certain what the output will be.

The clearest way to test whether a relation is a function is to scan the ordered pairs, the table, or the graph, and check whether any input value repeats with two different output values. Take the relation (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6), and (4, 8). Every input, 1, 2, 3, and 4, appears exactly once, so this relation is a function; it happens to follow the rule multiply the input by 2. Now compare that to the relation (1, 2), (1, 5), (3, 6), and (4, 8). Here the input 1 shows up twice, once paired with 2 and once paired with 5. That single repeated input with two different outputs breaks the rule, so this relation is not a function.

On a graph, this same idea becomes a quick visual check called the vertical line test. If you can draw any vertical line through the graph and it only ever touches the curve at one point, the graph represents a function, because a vertical line captures every point sharing one particular x-value, and touching only once means that x-value has only one paired y-value. A circle, for example, fails this test: a vertical line drawn through the middle of a circle crosses it at two points, top and bottom, meaning one x-value is paired with two different y-values, so a circle is not the graph of a function. A straight line that is not perfectly vertical, on the other hand, always passes the vertical line test, since any vertical line crosses it exactly once.

It is worth being precise about the direction of the rule, because it is easy to mix up. Outputs are allowed to repeat across different inputs; that causes no problem at all. The relation (1, 5), (2, 5), (3, 5) is still a function, even though every single output is 5, because each input still only maps to that one output. What breaks the rule is a repeated input mapped to different outputs, never a repeated output.

This distinction between relations and functions is why the concept of function sits right after relation in this sequence: a function narrows the wide category of relations down to the dependable ones, and every idea that follows, domain, range, input, output, function notation, and evaluating functions, depends on that dependable, one-output-per-input structure holding true.
